newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: LME aluminium squeeze tricky, China buys zinc calls.
newsitem.headline: LME aluminium squeeze tricky, China buys zinc calls.

text.p: Three-month aluminium prices were barely changed on Thursday in Asian trade despite some talk the metal is in the the process of undergoing a market squeeze.

"Aluminium prices are expected to consolidate in a range between $1,650 and $1,700 and then will see a correction as technical indicators show the market is overbought," said a metal trader at a major trading house.

The 14-day relative strength index (RSI) for three-month aluminium stood at 74.92 percent on Wednesday from 76.38 percent the previous day. The market generally considers an RSI of 70 or more as overbought and 30 or less as oversold.

LME broker Macquarie said in its daily report three-month aluminium prices have climbed by 10 percent from the bottom of their recent trading range ($1,500 a tonne), breaking through the top of the range ($1,700) at the start of this week.

Macquarie said the target of the squeeze was believed to be traders who hold large volumes of uncovered call options at $1,700 a tonne. The main tightness appeared to be centred around the August prompt date, and then November's date. The backwardation between November and December was $13 a tonne.

But the broker argued the level of unreported or "hidden" aluminium stocks, which could amount to as much as 500,000 tonnes and have been financed by banks using the contango, would prevent any successful attempt to squeeze the market.
With prices having swung into backwardation, stocks would be released to the market as refinancing would no longer be possible, Macquarie said.

The other danger for the "squeeze" was that higher prices could prove too tempting for producers' and prompt the restart of idled smelting capacity, currently estimated at 780,000 tonnes a year worldwide.
There have been unconfirmed rumours that Alcoa has begun hiring staff in preparation for restarts, Macquarie said.

Meanwhile, London Metal Exchange (LME) zinc is likely to see more volatility before September as the battle between short Chinese smelters, and traders and funds holding longs positions continues, dealers said.
Three-month zinc prices were flat at $1,440 at 0500 GMT in thin Asian trade from the previous day's close.
"The widening zinc backwardation on Wednesday was mainly due to short-covering and borrowing, widely believed to be coming from the Chinese," one Korean trader said,
He said the smelters seem to have rolled over their nearby shorts to the first quarter of next year to earn more time to produce physical zinc.
Traders said the Chinese seem to have used several strategies to avoid further losses in the zinc market.

"The first was to buy call options to lock in their losses, and the second was to buy three-month zinc futures to adjust existing nearby positions by borrowing, or to borrow existing loss-bearing shorts for the next first quarter," a broker said.
"Another option was to buy zinc futures outright, but we believe they didn't need to do that as they could have locked in their losses by purchasing calls," the broker said.
Wednesday's zinc sell-off was sparked by funds who were caught by Tuesday's price collapse, a dealer said.
"There was not enough time for the funds to get out of their longs on Tuesday. Some funds were said to have liquidated their longs at around $1,530 a tonne yesterday," he added.
In the LME copper market, which fell sharply overnight, Chinese buyers were expected to hold back purchases unless three-month copper prices fall to around $2,200 a tonne.
"We expect the Chinese will buy copper at $2,200 a tonne, basis three-months," a trader said.
-- Jae Hur, Seoul Newsroom (822) 727 5651
